newsitem.title: POLAND: Small impact seen of free Polish fuel prices on CP.
newsitem.headline: Small impact seen of free Polish fuel prices on CP.

text.p: The freeing of Polish fuel prices on Thursday is an inflationary impulse, but should not add more than between 0.5 to one point to this year's government inflation targets, analysts said on Thursday.

The finance ministry announced it was freeing prices of fuels and removing all administrative limits on profit margins applied to engine fuel trade in leaded and unleaded petrol as well as diesel fuel as of February 13.
Maximum prices of domestically produced-fuel and distributors' profit margins on both imported and domestic fuel have so far been controlled by the finance ministry.

"The freeing of fuel prices will not have any significant effect on Poland's inflation targets for this year -- it may add up to 0.5 point to 1997 goals," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, chief analyst at the government Centre for Strategic Studies.

The government wants to bring inflation down to 13 percent in year-on-year terms at the end of this year from 18.5 percent in December 1996. The average annual inflation target is 15 percent for 1997 against 19.9 in 1996.
"The move may add up a point at the most to Poland's inflation this year which doesn't worry me at all," said Andrew Kennigham, analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.
Several other analysts said inflation could increase some 0.2-0.3 point as a result of the move.
The ministry also scrapped a regulation obliging fuel producers and distributors to inform tax offices of price rises in advance, which could then be held up for three months.
Despite an average jump of 35 percent of the world oil prices in 1996, the ministry had been reluctant to let domestic prices rise, fearing a strong inflationary impulse.
As a result, Polish refineries suffered reduced profits because they could not offset the rising world crude prices by increasing domestic market prices -- held down by the ministry.

Poland's biggest Plock refinery already said it would raise its prices of fuel but was still analysing the scope of the rise while the second biggest Gdansk refinery said it would raise its prices as of February 14 by between five and 8.5 percent.
Analysts said fuel prices at filling stations could at first rise by an average of about seven percent, but could then fall as a result of fierce competition between distributors.

"At first prices will rise, which is natural, but then they should stabilise with a downward inclination because we will see the benefits of competition," said Bogdan Wyznikiewicz, head of the independent Gdansk economic think-tank. "After that prices will depend on the size of the excise tax and the situation on world oil markets," he said.
However, some said the competition may prove difficult as 50 percent of Poland's petrol and diesel sales were in the hands of the biggest fuel distributor, the state-owned CPN SA.

"The competition may be difficult considering CPN's market share. Also the refineries may find it easier to reach some kind of consensus on prices than to fight each other," said Piotr Las, analyst at Creditanstalt Securities in Warsaw.

The freeing of fuel prices is the key to the lagging restructuring and privatisation of the oil sector, which has to modernise before it faces though foreign competition when Poland lifts barriers protecting the market in three years time.
